overview: Tarbosaurus bataar was the apex predator of the Late Cretaceous Nemegt Formation of Mongolia (~70 Ma) — the Asian ecological equivalent of Tyrannosaurus, reaching similar size and filling an identical predatory role in a contemporaneous but geographically distinct ecosystem. Its skull is proportionally even narrower than T. rex and its forelimbs particularly reduced.

Whether Tarbosaurus should be synonymised with Tyrannosaurus (as T. bataar) has been debated since the 1990s. Most current analyses treat them as separate genera based on consistent skull proportions, biogeography and the principle that combining them would require unexplained intercontinental dispersal. The Beringian land bridge may have allowed some exchange, but differences between the two are well supported.

articles.title: Discovery and taxonomy
articles.body: Described by Maleev in 1955 from Mongolian material collected by Soviet expeditions, Tarbosaurus bataar has been the subject of repeated synonymy debates with Tyrannosaurus. Modern phylogenetic and morphological analyses consistently recover them as sister taxa or close relatives but distinct genera — the current consensus. A smuggled Tarbosaurus skeleton sold at US auction in 2012 was seized and returned to Mongolia after legal action.

articles.title: Anatomy
articles.body: The skull is proportionally narrow with a strongly kinetic palate and binocular vision comparable to T. rex. The forelimbs are proportionally even smaller than in T. rex, and the hand has just two functional fingers. Bone texture studies indicate some very large specimens were still growing at death.

articles.title: Nemegt ecosystem
articles.body: The Nemegt Formation records a warm, well-watered floodplain with rivers, lakes and seasonal drought. Tarbosaurus preyed on giant hadrosaurs (Saurolophus, Barsboldia) and sauropods (Nemegtosaurus), in addition to smaller ornithischians. Alioramus may have occupied a different prey niche in the same ecosystem.

record.description: Tarbosaurus bataar was a large tyrannosaurine from the Nemegt Formation of Mongolia, known from numerous skulls and skeletons across growth stages.
facts: Most current analyses retain Tarbosaurus as distinct from Tyrannosaurus, though the combination Tyrannosaurus bataar has historical use.
Juveniles had proportionally longer, lower skulls and changed feeding mechanics through growth.

presentation.heroLead: The giant tyrannosaurine of Late Cretaceous Mongolia, known from dozens of skulls and skeletons that span the growth from small juveniles to twelve-metre adults.

animalParagraphs: Tarbosaurus was a very large two-legged predator and the biggest carnivore of the Nemegt ecosystem. The largest individuals are estimated at ten to twelve metres long and several tonnes in mass, a little smaller than the largest Tyrannosaurus. The skull is deep but narrower than that of its North American cousin, with a locking joint between the upper jaw bones that stiffened the snout.

Its arms were the shortest relative to body size of any tyrannosaurid, ending in two-fingered hands. The braincase preserves natural casts showing large olfactory regions, consistent with a strong sense of smell, while the eyes faced more sideways than in Tyrannosaurus.

Juveniles were slender, long-legged animals with low, narrow skulls and blade-like teeth, and adults became far more robust. That transformation, documented by a two- to three-year-old skeleton, means Tarbosaurus probably occupied different feeding roles at different stages of life. Bite marks on hadrosaur and sauropod bones from the Nemegt Formation are usually attributed to it, but which animal made them cannot be proven.
animalHighlights: A deep, narrow skull with a rigid snout and a distinctive locking mechanism between the maxilla and the jugal bones.
The proportionally smallest forelimbs of any tyrannosaurid, ending in two functional fingers.
One of the most complete tyrannosaurid growth series known, from a juvenile a few years old to full-sized adults.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by teeth, jaws and bite marks
lifeCards.reason: Thick serrated teeth and a heavily built skull indicate a predator or scavenger of large animals. Tooth-marked Saurolophus and sauropod bones from the same rocks are consistent with, but do not prove, Tarbosaurus feeding.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Complete hindlimbs are preserved in several individuals. Adult speed is not measurable from bone and biomechanical estimates vary.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Length is constrained by near-complete adult skeletons; mass estimates of roughly four to five tonnes depend on the modelling method.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Proportions come from articulated skeletons. Scaly skin is inferred from impressions in related tyrannosaurids rather than from Tarbosaurus itself; colour is unknown.

whereFacts.label: Type locality
whereFacts.value: Tsagan Khushu, Nemegt Basin, Ömnögovi, Mongolia

locality.name: Nemegt Basin
locality.note: Nemegt Formation. The holotype skull was collected by the Soviet–Mongolian expedition of 1946; many later specimens come from Nemegt, Altan Uul, Bugiin Tsav and neighbouring localities.

presentation.classificationSummary: Tarbosaurus is a tyrannosaurine tyrannosaurid, the Asian sister taxon of Tyrannosaurus in most analyses. Some workers treat it as a species of Tyrannosaurus (T. bataar); most keep the genera separate on cranial differences, and the question remains open.

related.reason: Its closest relative, from North America; some authors place the two in a single genus.
A smaller, long-snouted tyrannosaurine that shared the Nemegt landscape with adult Tarbosaurus.
A North American tyrannosaurine sometimes recovered close to the Tarbosaurus–Tyrannosaurus lineage.

questions.title: Is Tarbosaurus really a separate genus?
questions.copy: Tarbosaurus and Tyrannosaurus differ in skull architecture and forelimb proportions, but they are very close relatives. Whether that difference merits a separate genus is a judgement rather than a fact, and Tyrannosaurus bataar has been used by some authors.

questions.title: What did the juveniles eat?
questions.copy: The two- to three-year-old skeleton MPC-D 107/7 has a slender skull and blade-like teeth unlike those of adults, so juveniles probably took smaller, different prey. The exact diet is not preserved.

questions.title: How many species are in the sample?
questions.copy: Several names were once applied to Mongolian tyrannosaurids of different sizes. Most are now read as growth stages of one species, but the small number of well-studied juveniles leaves some room for doubt.

specimens.note: Partial skull with vertebrae collected at Tsagan Khushu in 1946; named Tyrannosaurus bataar by Maleev in 1955.

specimens.name: Juvenile skeleton
specimens.note: Nearly complete skull and partial skeleton of a two- to three-year-old individual described by Tsuihiji et al. in 2011.

panel.headline: Dozens of skulls and skeletons from the Gobi, spanning juvenile to adult growth stages.
panel.standfirst: Tarbosaurus bataar is one of the best-sampled large theropods. Soviet, Polish, Mongolian and Japanese expeditions have recovered more than thirty specimens from the Nemegt Formation, including near-complete adults and a small juvenile skeleton.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is known from several individuals, several skeletons are nearly complete, and a growth series from a two- to three-year-old to old adults is documented.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete skulls with dentition and braincases, full vertebral columns, ribs and gastralia, pectoral and pelvic girdles, both forelimbs with two-fingered hands, complete hindlimbs and feet, from small juveniles to the largest adults.
knownRemains.note: A large proportion of the specimens were collected before modern excavation standards and some are held far from their type locality, so provenance details for older material can be imprecise.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many complete skulls with teeth, palates and braincases; a natural brain endocast; the juvenile skull of MPC-D 107/7.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series with ribs, gastralia and chevrons in several mounted skeletons.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Pectoral and pelvic girdles, the proportionally tiny two-fingered forelimbs, complete hindlimbs and feet.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Natural braincase casts and healed injuries are known. No confirmed skin impressions, feathers, colour or gut contents belong to Tarbosaurus itself.

specimenCards.title: PIN 551-1 · holotype
specimenCards.description: A partial skull with some vertebrae collected at Tsagan Khushu in 1946 and named Tyrannosaurus bataar by Evgeny Maleev in 1955. Maleev's other Mongolian names, including Tarbosaurus efremovi, were later synonymised with it.

specimenCards.title: MPC-D 107/7
specimenCards.description: A nearly complete skull and partial skeleton of an individual estimated at two to three years old, described in 2011. It shows a low, slender skull and blade-like teeth very different from the adult condition.
specimenCards.meta: Bugiin Tsav · Nemegt Formation · Mongolian Palaeontological Center, Ulaanbaatar

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Numerous skulls and skeletons across a growth series, a natural brain cast, and tooth-marked prey bones from the same formation.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: The top predator of the Nemegt fauna, with juveniles and adults occupying different feeding roles as skull shape and teeth changed with growth.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Whether it should be sunk into Tyrannosaurus, the external covering and colour, adult speed, and exactly which animals made the recorded bite marks.
